stemMd:
The language of the Pell Islands, Ressan, has its own words for most farm tools and crops, but nearly all of its words for boats, nets, and sea fish are borrowed from Torvan, the language spoken along the nearby mainland coast. Linguist Oskar Nyberg notes that a language usually borrows its words for things that its speakers first learned about from speakers of another language. Historical records also show that until the eighteenth century, Ressan speakers lived only in the islands' inland valleys, far from the shore. Taken together, these facts suggest that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Ressan probably borrowed its words for farm tools and crops from a language other than Torvan.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Ressan speakers probably took up fishing at sea only after they came into contact with Torvan speakers.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Ressan speakers probably moved from the coast to the inland valleys to avoid conflict with Torvan speakers.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Torvan speakers probably learned to farm from Ressan speakers after settling in the Pell Islands.

explanationMd:
An inference item gives you premises and asks for the conclusion they jointly support. List them:

1. Ressan's sea and fishing words (boats, nets, sea fish) are almost all borrowed from Torvan.
2. Languages usually borrow words for things their speakers first learned about from another group.
3. Ressan speakers lived inland, away from the sea, until the eighteenth century.

Premises 1 and 2 together suggest that Ressan speakers learned about boats, nets and sea fish from Torvan speakers; premise 3 makes that likely, since an inland people would have had little sea fishing of its own. The conclusion that they took up sea fishing only after contact with Torvan speakers follows.

Check the rest against the premises. The text says nothing about Torvan speakers borrowing anything, or about Torvan speakers settling in the islands. The records place Ressan speakers inland all along, not moving inland from the coast. And Ressan has its *own* words for farm tools, so they were not borrowed at all.

distractorRationale.d: The text describes only words flowing from Torvan into Ressan. Nothing indicates that Torvan speakers settled in the islands or learned farming from anyone, so this reverses the direction of the evidence.
distractorRationale.c: The records say Ressan speakers lived inland until the eighteenth century, not that they moved there from the coast, and the text gives no evidence of conflict.
distractorRationale.a: The text says Ressan has its own words for most farm tools and crops, so the premise that they were borrowed from any language contradicts the passage.

accessibilityText: A short linguistics passage. Ressan, the language of the Pell Islands, has its own words for most farm tools and crops, but nearly all its words for boats, nets and sea fish are borrowed from Torvan, the language of the nearby mainland coast. Linguist Oskar Nyberg notes that a language usually borrows words for things its speakers first learned about from speakers of another language. Records show that until the eighteenth century Ressan speakers lived only in the islands' inland valleys, far from the shore. The final sentence reads: taken together, these facts suggest that, blank. The choices are: Ressan probably borrowed its words for farm tools and crops from a language other than Torvan; Ressan speakers probably took up fishing at sea only after they came into contact with Torvan speakers; Ressan speakers probably moved from the coast to the inland valleys to avoid conflict with Torvan speakers; and Torvan speakers probably learned to farm from Ressan speakers after settling in the Pell Islands.

provenance.notes: Original inference item. The Pell Islands, the Ressan and Torvan languages and Nyberg's observation are invented; the key requires combining all three premises.

independentSolve.workingNotes: Sea-related words borrowed from Torvan plus the principle that borrowed words name things learned from other speakers, plus Ressan speakers living inland until the 18th century, suggest they took up sea fishing only after contact with Torvan speakers. Ressan has its own farm words, so borrowing them is contradicted; moving from coast to valleys reverses the record; Torvan speakers learning farming is unsupported. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: Ressan borrowed sea-related words from Torvan, borrowing signals things learned from other speakers, and Ressan speakers lived inland until the 1700s, so they likely learned sea fishing from Torvan speakers. Ressan has its own farm words, so no borrowing there; there is no evidence they moved from coast to inland or that Torvan speakers learned farming from them.]
